units.text: 10. More than the sum of particles

Saying that a novel consists of characters is true. Saying that understanding the alphabet suffices to explain betrayal in the novel is absurd. Yet the fictional characters require no additional letters outside the text. The example shows that dependence on a substrate and explanatory sufficiency of the substrate’s vocabulary are not the same thing.

‘Reductionism’ designates several theses. One is ontological: everything in the domain discussed depends on physical components and their relations. Another is methodological: to understand, we break the system into parts and investigate mechanisms. A third is explanatory: all good explanations can be replaced without significant loss by explanations at the lowest level. We can accept the second’s usefulness without having proved the first, and accept the first without being committed to the third.

A molecular explanation of a substance may be indispensable for one question and needlessly detailed for another. If I want to know why a bridge collapsed, I may need material properties, geometry, loads and maintenance history. Even an available complete list of particles does not automatically tell me which comparisons matter for design and responsibility.

Think of a program bug. It is physically realized by circuits and memory. But the explanation ‘this branch does not handle the zero case’ may identify the problem better than a description of every electrical switching event. We invoke no supernatural power of software. We choose a level at which regularity and intervention are intelligible.

The same principle helps us discuss top-down causation without mysticism. A channel’s shape constrains water flow. The channel’s geometry is realized through matter; it does not come from outside physics. Yet to explain the difference between two flows, the relevant variable may be shape rather than the complete microscopic inventory. Some debates on emergent causation pursue a stronger thesis, but the ordinary example of constraints does not prove it alone.

The critic of reductionism is right to demand attention to organization, context and levels. They are wrong to think ‘the whole’ explains something before specifying through which relations it does so. A sentence such as ‘the system has a holistic energy’ does not become an explanation merely because it sounds more generous than the vocabulary of mechanisms. It must show effects, conditions and observable differences.

There is also a mathematical argument against an overly naive reduction: knowing microscopic rules does not guarantee a general algorithm answering all macroscopic questions. Gu and colleagues construct models in which certain properties of infinite systems are undecidable. The result has technical premises and does not automatically transfer to every finite material, but it destroys the simple inference ‘known rules, therefore every property can be computed’ (Gu et al., 2009) .

It does not follow that the higher level introduces new matter. It follows that ontological reduction, if true, is not the same as having a computational method or short explanation available. We may live in a world entirely dependent on a few rules and still need different disciplines to understand it.

Rigorous pluralism does not put all explanations on an equal footing. Biological explanation must be compatible with relevant physical constraints; economic explanation cannot ignore resources; psychological explanation cannot turn every adverse result into confirmation. But compatibility does not require eliminating the vocabulary of functions, information, institutions and motives.

The useful question is not ‘are you a reductionist or a holist?’ as though choosing a camp. It is: for this problem, which details are necessary, which relationships are robust and which intervention would distinguish the explanations? Sometimes we must descend to components. At other times we must raise our gaze until we see the configuration that makes them relevant.

A world of simple rules is not necessarily a world with simple explanations for every question. This may be the most important correction to the dream of a ‘theory of everything’: even if we obtained an extraordinary fundamental theory, we would still have to discover what happens when everything is put together.
